claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal-dominant hereditary neurodegenerative disorder caused by a pathogenic expansion of the CAG trinucleotide repeats in exon 1 of the huntingtin (HTT) gene.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal-dominant hereditary neurodegenerative disorder caused by a pathogenic expansion of the CAG trinucleotide repeats in exon 1 of the huntingtin (HTT) gene (A novel gene containing a trinucleotide repeat that is expanded and unstable on Huntington's disease chromosomes. The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to The Huntington's Disease Collaborative Research Group, 1993, which is a foundational reference for HD genetics.

claim: The clinical features of HD include motor deficit, psychiatric disturbance, cognitive impairment, and peripheral signs such as weight loss and sleep disturbance.
source: The clinical features of HD include motor deficit, psychiatric disturbance, cognitive impairment, and peripheral signs such as weight loss and sleep disturbance (Ghosh and Tabrizi, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ghosh and Tabrizi, 2015, which describes the clinical features of HD.

claim: Disease onset in HD is dependent on the CAG repeat length.
source: Disease onset, which is dependent on the CAG repeat length, is usually defined by the onset of motor symptoms, although non-motor symptoms are often present many years in advance.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the relationship between CAG repeat length and disease onset in HD.

claim: The striking neuropathological characteristic of HD is the progressive brain atrophy mainly in the striatum and cerebral cortex.
source: The striking neuropathological characteristic of HD, induced by the mutant Htt protein (mHtt), is the progressive brain atrophy mainly in the striatum and cerebral cortex (Walker, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walker, 2007, which describes the neuropathological characteristics of HD.

claim: The primary vulnerable neuronal types in HD are medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum and pyramidal neurons in the cortex.
source: Despite ubiquitously expressed mHtt protein in HD brain, the primary vulnerable neuronal types are medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum and pyramidal neurons in the cortex (Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998, which identifies the vulnerable neuronal types in HD.

claim: Widespread mHtt protein aggregation in HD brain tissue is a hallmark of HD pathology.
source: Widespread mHtt protein aggregation in HD brain tissue is another hallmark of HD pathology (Davies and Scherzinger, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davies and Scherzinger, 1997, which describes mHtt protein aggregation as a hallmark of HD.

claim: The causative gene for HD was identified 28 years ago.
source: While the causative gene for HD was identified 28 years ago (Macdonald, 1993), there are still no effective disease-modifying therapies available to prevent or delay the progression of this disorder.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Macdonald, 1993, which marks the identification of the HD gene.

claim: There are still no effective disease-modifying therapies available to prevent or delay the progression of HD.
source: While the causative gene for HD was identified 28 years ago (Macdonald, 1993), there are still no effective disease-modifying therapies available to prevent or delay the progression of this disorder.
evidence: This claim is based on the current state of HD therapeutics as stated in the manuscript.

claim: BAC226Q mice were generated using a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) system expressing full-length human HTT with ~226 CAG-CAA repeats.
source: Here, we report the generation and characterization of a novel Huntington's disease (HD) mouse model BAC226Q by using a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) system, expressing full-length human HTT with ~226 CAG-CAA repeats and containing endogenous human HTT promoter and regulatory elements.
evidence: This claim describes the generation method of the BAC226Q mouse model as reported in the manuscript.

claim: BAC226Q mice contain endogenous human HTT promoter and regulatory elements.
source: Here, we report the generation and characterization of a novel Huntington's disease (HD) mouse model BAC226Q by using a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) system, expressing full-length human HTT with ~226 CAG-CAA repeats and containing endogenous human HTT promoter and regulatory elements.
evidence: This claim describes the genetic construct used in the BAC226Q mouse model.

claim: BAC226Q mice recapitulated a full-spectrum of age-dependent and progressive HD-like phenotypes without unwanted and erroneous phenotypes.
source: BAC226Q recapitulated a full-spectrum of age-dependent and progressive HD-like phenotypes without unwanted and erroneous phenotypes.
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall characterization of the BAC226Q mouse model as presented in the manuscript.

claim: BAC226Q mice developed normally.
source: BAC226Q mice developed normally, and gradually exhibited HD-like psychiatric and cognitive phenotypes at 2 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BAC226Q mice gradually exhibited HD-like psychiatric and cognitive phenotypes at 2 months.
source: BAC226Q mice developed normally, and gradually exhibited HD-like psychiatric and cognitive phenotypes at 2 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript for 2-month-old mice.

claim: From 3 to 4 months, BAC226Q mice showed robust progressive motor deficits.
source: From 3 to 4 months, BAC226Q mice showed robust progressive motor deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by motor behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed gradual weight loss.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurement data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice exhibited significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuropathological data including MRI and stereological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice exhibited striatal neuronal death.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological neuron counting data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice exhibited widespread huntingtin inclusions.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data showing huntingtin aggregates presented in the manuscript.

claim: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice exhibited reactive pathology.
source: At 11 months, BAC226Q mice showed significant reduced life span, gradual weight loss and exhibited neuropathology including significant brain atrophy specific to striatum and cortex, striatal neuronal death, widespread huntingtin inclusions, and reactive pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by GFAP immunostaining data showing reactive gliosis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two copies of the human HTT were inserted in chromosome 8 in FVB mouse genome at Chr8:46084002.
source: To determine the copy number and insertion sites in FVB mouse genome of full-length human HTT, whole-genome sequencing was applied and indicated two copies of the human HTT were inserted in the chromosome 8 in FVB mouse genome at Chr8:46084002 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The band for 226Q mutant huntingtin in BAC226Q mouse is at a higher molecular weight than that for 97Q huntingtin in the BACHD mouse.
source: As expected, the band for 226Q mutant huntingtin in BAC226Q mouse is at a higher molecular weight than that for 97Q huntingtin in the BACHD mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There are no Htt protein fragments detected in 2- or 11-month BAC226Q mouse in Western blots.
source: There are no Htt protein fragments detected in 2- or 11-month BAC226Q mouse in Western blots (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both male and female transgenic BAC226Q mice were born in the expected Mendelian ratios with no obvious abnormalities.
source: Both male and female transgenic mice were born in the expected Mendelian ratios with no obvious abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on breeding observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: Both male and female BAC226Q mice were fertile.
source: Both males and females were fertile, but males were preferred for breeding because female animals had a short window of time during which they were able to adequately care for pups.
evidence: This claim is based on breeding observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: Female BAC226Q mice had a short window of time during which they were able to adequately care for pups.
source: Both males and females were fertile, but males were preferred for breeding because female animals had a short window of time during which they were able to adequately care for pups.
evidence: This claim is based on breeding observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: Only 50% of transgenic BAC226Q animals survive past 1 year in both sexes.
source: Transgenic BAC226Q mice had significantly reduced lifespan (Figure 2A). In both sexes, only 50% of transgenic animals survive past 1 year.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The longest surviving transgenic BAC226Q mice were 15 months old when they had to be euthanized due to the end-point condition according to animal welfare requirements.
source: The longest surviving transgenic mice were 15 months old when they had to be euthanized due to the end-point condition according to animal welfare requirements.
evidence: This claim is based on survival data reported in the manuscript.

claim: Non-transgenic littermate controls appeared healthy at 15 months of age.
source: In comparison, non-transgenic littermate controls appeared healthy at 15 months of age.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data reported in the manuscript.

claim: BAC226Q mice were born normal and gained weight at the same rate as their non-transgenic littermates in the developmental stage.
source: Animal weights were recorded weekly and the results show that HD mice were born normal and gained weight at the same rate as their non-transgenic littermates in the developmental stage (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurement data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In both male and female WT littermates, body weight continuously increased until the 11 months of age.
source: In both male and female WT littermates, body weight continuously increased until the 11 months of age; however, BAC226Q exhibited slower weight gain followed by progressive and significant weight loss which resulted in about 40% loss at 11 months (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurement data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: BAC226Q mice exhibited slower weight gain followed by progressive and significant weight loss which resulted in about 40% loss at 11 months.
source: In both male and female WT littermates, body weight continuously increased until the 11 months of age; however, BAC226Q exhibited slower weight gain followed by progressive and significant weight loss which resulted in about 40% loss at 11 months (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by weight measurement data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Weight loss is a common and serious complication in HD patients, who fail to maintain weight even when caloric intake is increased.
source: Weight loss is a common and serious complication in HD patients, who fail to maintain weight even when caloric intake is increased (Aziz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aziz et al., 2008, which describes weight loss in HD patients.

claim: BAC226Q mice recapitulated the weight loss aspect of HD accurately.
source: BAC226Q mice recapitulated this aspect accurately.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of weight loss data in BAC226Q mice with the known weight loss phenotype in HD patients.

claim: The earliest, most visible motor phenotype in the BAC226Q mice was the chorea-like movement which first manifested between 12 and 14 weeks.
source: The earliest, most visible motor phenotype in the BAC226Q mice was the chorea-like movement which first manifested between 12 and 14 weeks.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data of motor phenotypes reported in the manuscript.

claim: The motor phenotypes in BAC226Q mice include abrupt unnatural jerking and twisting of the head and body, resembling the chorea movement in HD patients.
source: The motor phenotypes include abrupt unnatural jerking and twisting of the head and body (Video 1), resembling the chorea movement in HD patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by video documentation (Video 1) and comparison to HD patient symptoms.

claim: Every transgenic BAC226Q mouse exhibits HD-like movement.
source: It should be noted that every transgenic BAC226Q mouse exhibits this HD-like movement.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data reported in the manuscript.

claim: Between 14 and 16 weeks, rapid circling behavior appeared in BAC226Q mice, and was especially prominent when animals were disturbed in their cages.
source: Between 14 and 16 weeks, rapid circling behavior appeared, and was especially prominent when animals were disturbed in their cages (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by video documentation (Video 2) and observational data.

claim: At 2 months, BAC226Q mice are indistinguishable from non-transgenic littermate controls in both horizontal and vertical activity measures in the open field task.
source: At 2 months, HD mice are indistinguishable from non-transgenic littermate controls in both horizontal and vertical activity measures.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Horizontal activity is dramatically increased at 4 months in BAC226Q mice.
source: Horizontal activity is dramatically increased at 4 months (Figure 3A), but returns to wild-type levels at 10 and 15 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Horizontal activity returns to wild-type levels at 10 and 15 months in BAC226Q mice.
source: Horizontal activity is dramatically increased at 4 months (Figure 3A), but returns to wild-type levels at 10 and 15 months.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Vertical activity of 4-month BAC226Q mice has declined to about 20% of the controls.
source: In contrast, vertical activity of 4-month HD mice has declined to about 20% of the controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 10 and 15 months, horizontal activity is reduced to wild-type levels but vertical activity does not recover and becomes even more impaired in BAC226Q mice.
source: While reduced vertical activity at 4 months may be caused by the increase in horizontal movement, at 10 and 15 months, horizontal activity is reduced to wild-type levels but vertical activity does not recover and becomes even more impaired.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field test data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The motor symptom progression in BAC226Q mice parallels the biphasic motor symptom progression in HD patients in which early stage involuntary movements become more dystonic in late stages of disease.
source: These results parallel the biphasic motor symptom progression in HD patients in which early stage involuntary movements become more dystonic in late stages of disease.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of motor phenotype data in BAC226Q mice with known HD patient symptom progression.

claim: Rearing frequency is unchanged in BAC226Q mice at 2 and 4 months in the cylinder test.
source: Similar to the open field test, BAC226Q mice are normal at 2 months and defective at 4 months in the cylinder test (Video 3). At 4 months, rearing frequency was unchanged, but rearing time was significantly reduced (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cylinder test data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Rearing time was significantly reduced at 4 months in BAC226Q mice in the cylinder test.
source: Similar to the open field test, BAC226Q mice are normal at 2 months and defective at 4 months in the cylinder test (Video 3). At 4 months, rearing frequency was unchanged, but rearing time was significantly reduced (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cylinder test data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The transgenic BAC226Q mice retained their instinct to rear to explore the environment, but were unable to sustain upright posture due to motor impairment.
source: These results suggest that the transgenic mice retained their instinct to rear to explore the environment, but were unable to sustain upright posture due to motor impairment.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the cylinder test data showing unchanged rearing frequency but reduced rearing time.

claim: The frequency of turning was significantly increased over controls in BAC226Q mice in the cylinder test.
source: While BAC226Q mice spent time turning in both directions, and the frequency of turning was significantly increased over controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by cylinder test data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Circling in BAC226Q mice may be explained by a reduced capacity to inhibit or terminate movements such as turns.
source: Circling in BAC226Q mice may be explained by a reduced capacity to inhibit or terminate movements such as turns.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the circling behavior observed in BAC226Q mice.

claim: No differences between BAC226Q and controls could be detected in the accelerating rotarod test until 12 weeks.
source: Consistent with the open field and cylinder results, no differences between BAC226Q and controls could be detected until 12 weeks (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At 13 weeks, BAC226Q mice performed significantly worse compared to non-transgenic controls in the accelerating rotarod test.
source: At 13 weeks, BAC226Q mice performed significantly worse compared to non-transgenic controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At 16 weeks, BAC226Q mice were unable to balance on the rotarod for any duration of time.
source: At 16 weeks, BAC226Q mice were unable to balance on the rotarod for any duration of time.
evidence: This claim is supported by rotarod test data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In HD patients, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms are common and as detrimental to quality of life as motor disorders.
source: In HD patients, cognitive and psychiatric symptoms are common and as detrimental to quality of life as motor disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HD symptoms.

claim: There is evidence of impaired hippocampal function in pre-symptomatic HD patients.
source: Because there is an evidence of impaired hippocampal function in pre-symptomatic HD patients, we chose a challenging cognitive task with a hippocampus-dependent spatial component (Phillips et al., 2008; Ransome et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2008 and Ransome et al., 2012.

claim: BAC226Q mice showed no discrimination of the moved objects in the object-in-place memory test.
source: BAC226Q mice, on the other hand, showed no discrimination of the moved objects (Figure 4A) despite spent an equal total amount of time exploring the objects in both training and testing sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by object-in-place memory test data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BAC226Q mice spent an equal total amount of time exploring the objects in both training and testing sessions in the object-in-place memory test.
source: BAC226Q mice, on the other hand, showed no discrimination of the moved objects (Figure 4A) despite spent an equal total amount of time exploring the objects in both training and testing sessions.
evidence: This claim is based on object-in-place memory test data reported in the manuscript.

claim: The BAC226Q mice have impairments in hippocampal-dependent cognitive function at 2 months.
source: These results suggest that the BAC226Q mice have impairments in hippocampal-dependent cognitive function at 2 months.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the object-in-place memory test data.

claim: Depression and anhedonia are common in HD patients.
source: Depression and anhedonia are also common in HD patients.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HD symptoms.

claim: While non-transgenic littermates preferred the sucrose solution, BAC226Q mice showed significantly reduced preference in the sucrose preference task.
source: While non-transgenic littermates preferred the sucrose solution, BAC226Q mice showed significantly reduced preference (Figure 4B), indicating an anhedonia-like phenotype typical of depression.
evidence: This claim is supported by sucrose preference test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BAC226Q mice showed an anhedonia-like phenotype typical of depression in the sucrose preference task.
source: While non-transgenic littermates preferred the sucrose solution, BAC226Q mice showed significantly reduced preference (Figure 4B), indicating an anhedonia-like phenotype typical of depression.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the sucrose preference test data and comparison to depression phenotypes.

claim: BAC226Q mice spent significantly less time grooming compared to non-transgenic littermate in the splash test.
source: When sprayed with a sticky sucrose solution, BAC226Q mice spent significantly less time grooming compared to non-transgenic littermate (Figure 4C), demonstrating further a depression-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by splash test data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BAC226Q mice demonstrated a depression-like behavior in the splash test.
source: When sprayed with a sticky sucrose solution, BAC226Q mice spent significantly less time grooming compared to non-transgenic littermate (Figure 4C), demonstrating further a depression-like behavior.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the splash test data and comparison to depression phenotypes.

claim: BAC226Q mice had three times higher immobility time than non-transgenic littermate controls in the forced swim task.
source: The results were highly significant that BAC226Q mice had three times higher immobility time than non-transgenic littermate controls (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by forced swim test data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The three tests indicated a range of depression-like phenotypes including disinterest in rewarding stimuli, apathy, and hopelessness in a stressful situation in BAC226Q mice.
source: Combined, these three tests indicated a range of depression-like phenotypes including disinterest in rewarding stimuli, apathy, and hopelessness in a stressful situation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results of the sucrose preference, splash, and forced swim tests.

claim: Post-mortem brains of HD patients have a significant reduction in brain volume, especially in the striatum and deep layer cortex.
source: Post-mortem brains of HD patients have a significant reduction in brain volume, especially in the striatum and deep layer cortex.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HD neuropathology.

claim: Age-dependent and progressive striatal atrophy and neuronal loss are cardinal neuropathology of HD patients that are well recapitulated in BAC226Q mice.
source: Age-dependent and progressive striatal atrophy and neuronal loss are cardinal neuropathology of HD patients that are well recapitulated in BAC226Q mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by neuropathological data shown in Figure 5A and subsequent panels.

claim: At 2 months, BAC226Q mice had similar brain weights compared to non-transgenic littermates.
source: At 2 months, BAC226Q mice had similar brain weights compared to non-transgenic littermates, and went through a progressive decrease.
evidence: This claim is supported by brain weight measurement data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 15 months, whole brains from surviving BAC226Q mice weighed 31% less than brains from non-transgenic littermate.
source: At 15 months, whole brains from surviving BAC226Q mice weighed 31% less than brains from non-transgenic littermate (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by brain weight measurement data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: BAC226Q striatal volume was significantly decreased by 34% compared to controls at 11 months.
source: The results showed that BAC226Q striatal volume was significantly decreased by 34% compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological volume measurement data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The volume of the ventricles in BAC226Q mice was greatly enlarged by 3.8-fold compared to that of the non-transgenic littermates at 11 months.
source: Additionally, similar to the enlarged brain ventricles in HD patients due to brain atrophy, the volume of the ventricles in BAC226Q mice was greatly enlarged by 3.8-fold compared to that of the non-transgenic littermates (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological volume measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: HD patients have enlarged brain ventricles due to brain atrophy.
source: Additionally, similar to the enlarged brain ventricles in HD patients due to brain atrophy, the volume of the ventricles in BAC226Q mice was greatly enlarged by 3.8-fold compared to that of the non-transgenic littermates (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HD neuropathology.

claim: The changes in striatal and ventricular volumes in BAC226Q mice closely mirrored the cardinal pathology in HD patient brains.
source: These changes in striatal and ventricular volumes closely mirrored the cardinal pathology in HD patient brains.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of neuropathological data in BAC226Q mice with known HD patient pathology.

claim: In human HD patients, striatal volume loss is attributed largely to the death of MSNs, which comprise 95% of neurons in the striatum.
source: In human HD patients, striatal volume loss is attributed largely to the death of MSNs, which comprise 95% of neurons in the striatum (Oorschot, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oorschot, 1996, which describes the composition of striatal neurons.

claim: At 2 months, no significant differences were detected between genotypes with an average striatal neuron population of 2,280,000±125,000 for non-transgenic and 2,174,000±127,000 for BAC226Q mice.
source: At 2 months, no significant differences were detected between genotypes with an average striatal neuron population of 2,280,000±125,000 for non-transgenic and 2,174,000±127,000 for HD mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological neuron counting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At 11 months, non-transgenic littermate control mice had an average of 1,988,000±193,000 striatal neurons, while BAC226Q mice had only 1,631,000±269,000, a difference of 18.0%.
source: However, at 11 months, non-transgenic littermate control mice had an average of 1,988,000±193,000 striatal neurons, while BAC226Q mice had only 1,631,000±269,000, a difference of 18.0% (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological neuron counting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DARPP-32 IOD was significantly reduced by 18.1% in BAC226Q striatum at 11 months of age.
source: DARPP-32 IOD was significantly reduced by 18.1% in BAC226Q striatum at 11 months of age (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DARPP-32 immunostaining quantification data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In 12-month transgenic BAC226Q mice, whole brain volume was 373.8±2.95 mm3, compared to 522.3±21.7 mm3 in non-transgenic controls, a decrease of 28.5%.
source: In 12-month transgenic BAC226Q mice, whole brain volume was 373.8±2.95 mm3, compared to 522.3±21.7 mm3 in non-transgenic controls, a decrease of 28.5% (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a statistically significant volume decrease in the cortex (24.8%, p=0.0113) in 12-month BAC226Q mice compared to controls.
source: We found statistically significant volume changes in several regions of the brain, including the cortex (24.8%, p=0.0113, Figure 6C) and striatum (19.4%, p=0.0453, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a statistically significant volume decrease in the striatum (19.4%, p=0.0453) in 12-month BAC226Q mice compared to controls.
source: We found statistically significant volume changes in several regions of the brain, including the cortex (24.8%, p=0.0113, Figure 6C) and striatum (19.4%, p=0.0453, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was a significant increase in the ventricle volume in the BAC226Q mice compared to non-transgenic littermate controls (206.8%, p<0.0001) at 12 months.
source: There was a significant increase in the ventricle volume in the BAC226Q mice compared to non-transgenic littermate controls (206.8%, p<0.0001, Figure 6E), which was consistent with the Cavalieri stereologic estimator data (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was no significant difference in cerebellar and amygdala volumes between genotypes at 12 months.
source: In contrast, there was no significant difference in cerebellar and amygdala volumes between genotypes (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figures 6F and 6G.

claim: The cerebellum and amygdala are largely unaffected in HD patients.
source: This is consistent with the observation that the cerebellum and amygdala are largely unaffected in HD patients.

claim: Other regions affected at 12 months in BAC226Q mice included cingulum, stria medullaris, anterior commissure, and corpus callosum/external capsule, suggesting a pronounced effect on white matter tracts.
source: Other regions affected at 12 months included cingulum, stria medullaris, anterior commissure, and corpus callosum/external capsule, suggesting a pronounced effect on white matter tracts (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by MRI volumetric analysis data shown in Figure 6H and represents an inference about white matter involvement.

claim: The detection of robust and progressive structural deficits as a biomarker by MRI provides a non-invasive and sensitive method for future therapeutic testing.
source: It is important to note that the detection of robust and progressive structural deficits as a biomarker by MRI provides a non-invasive and sensitive method for future therapeutic testing.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the MRI data and its potential application in therapeutic studies.

claim: In post-mortem HD brains, mHtt aggregations are found throughout the central nervous system as an important hallmark.
source: In post-mortem HD brains, mHtt aggregations are found throughout the central nervous system as an important hallmark (Mangiarini et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mangiarini et al., 1996, which describes mHtt aggregations in HD.

claim: Two types of huntingtin aggregates were observed in BAC226Q mice: nuclear inclusions (NIs) and neuropil aggregates (NAs).
source: In agreement with previous findings (Gray et al., 2008; Kazantsev et al., 1999; Li et al., 2001), two types of huntingtin aggregates were observed in BAC226Q mice, nuclear inclusions (NIs) and neuropil aggregates (NAs).

claim: At 2 months, neuron cell bodies were diffusely stained by the S830 antibody throughout the brain in BAC226Q mice, but no immunoreactivity detected in non-transgenic littermates.
source: At 2 months, neuron cell bodies were diffusely stained by the S830 antibody throughout the brain in BAC226Q mice (Figure 7A–F), but no immunoreactivity detected in non-transgenic littermates (Figure 7S-X).

claim: At 2 months only soluble mHtt protein is present in BAC226Q mice.
source: This suggests that at 2 months only soluble mHtt protein is present.

claim: Punctate staining of mHtt protein by S830 became evident in several regions of the brain at 4 months in BAC226Q mice, including striatum, motor and cingulate cortex, hippocampus and amygdala, but not control mice.
source: In contrast, punctate staining of mHtt protein by S830 became evident in several regions of the brain at 4 months, including striatum (Figure 7G), motor (Figure 7H) and cingulate cortex (Figure 7I), hippocampus (Figure 7J and K) and amygdala (Figure 7L) in BAC226Q mice, but not control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7.

claim: At 11 months, aggregate pathology was much more severe in BAC226Q mice.
source: At 11 months, aggregate pathology was much more severe in BAC226Q mice (Figure 7M–R).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Reactive gliosis is a cardinal pathology of HD in addition to selective neuronal loss.
